title_original: Asǝṭṭa: The Living Architecture of Memory at Morocco’s Venice Biennale 2026 Pavilion
excerpt_original: For Morocco’s national pavilion at the 61st International Art Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia, artist Amina Agueznay and curator Meriem Berrada present Asǝṭṭa, a monumental installation conceived for the Artiglierie in the Arsenale. Taking […]

blocks.text: For Morocco’s national pavilion at the 61st International Art Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia, artist Amina Agueznay and curator Meriem Berrada present Asǝṭṭa , a monumental installation conceived for the Artiglierie in the Arsenale. Taking its title from an Amazigh word for ritual weaving, the project grew from a collaboration between Agueznay and Berrada that began with Noise and developed through a 2018 weaving workshop in Assilah.

blocks.caption: Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa , installation view. Courtesy of the Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication of the Kingdom of Morocco © Matteo Losurdo

blocks.text: Wool, raffia and embroidered threads cascade from towering steel structures, their intricate surfaces bearing the imprint of generations of Moroccan artisans. Suspended between sculpture and architecture, these richly textured forms create an immersive landscape of shifting patterns and passageways, shaped by the contributions of 166 craftspeople from across the country. This is Asǝṭṭa , the monumental work by artist Amina Agueznay, curated by Meriem Berrada, presented as Morocco’s first official national pavilion at the 61st International Art Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia. Situated in the Arsenale, the pavilion marks a significant moment in Morocco’s institutional representation at the Biennale, placing the ingenuity and artistry of its craftspeople at the centre of an ambitious contemporary vision.

Taking its title from an Amazigh term associated with ritual weaving, Asǝṭṭa draws on traditions passed between generations, particularly among women whose skills have sustained cultural identities and connections to place. These practices preserve histories rarely captured in written archives, finding expression through material, gesture and collective memory. The work takes its architectural inspiration from the âatba , the threshold in Moroccan vernacular architecture, inviting visitors to experience the passage between the familiar and the unknown, private and public, tradition and experimentation.

The project builds on Agueznay and Berrada’s longstanding collaboration, which deepened through a workshop in Assilah in 2018. Their engagement with artisans has developed into a sustained exploration of the relationships between makers, materials and the communities in which their practices are rooted. Rather than treating craftsmanship as a static inheritance, Asǝṭṭa reveals its capacity for reinvention, challenging conventional distinctions between art and craft, individual authorship and collective creation. As Morocco establishes its official national presence at the Venice Biennale, the work offers a vision of cultural identity shaped by exchange, adaptation and the often-unacknowledged labour through which traditions remain alive.

For ART AFRICA , Suzette Bell-Roberts speaks with Amina Agueznay and Meriem Berrada about their collaboration, the artisans behind Asǝṭṭa , and the significance of presenting Morocco’s living cultural traditions within the international framework of the Venice Biennale. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa , installation view. Courtesy of the Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication of the Kingdom of Morocco © Matteo Losurdo

blocks.caption: Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa , installation view. Courtesy of the Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication of the Kingdom of Morocco © Matteo Losurdo

blocks.text: How has that history shaped Asǝṭṭa , and how have your roles as artist and curator influenced one another’s thinking?

Amina Agueznay: Meriem and I have worked together for a long time. Her curatorial focus lies at the intersection of contemporary art and craft, so our interests align. One project led to another, like beads on a string. From Curriculum Vitae ( What is Forgotten and What Remains , Musée de l’Immigration, Paris, 2021) to Fieldworks (solo exhibition, Loft Art Gallery, Marrakech, 2025), a red thread runs from each installation to the next, culminating in Asetta in Venice.

Meriem Berrada: Amina has influenced the way I curate, allowing the work to unfold at its own pace. I grew up in Fez, with a sensitivity to architecture and craftsmanship, but working with her taught me to look beyond a piece’s beauty or technical precision and focus on the thinking behind it. When we worked on bringing Noise to the MACAAL in 2018, she insisted we spend a day in Asilah, where it was made. The work could not be understood separately from those encounters. That has stayed with me. With Asǝtta, the curatorial work began long before there was a finished installation to organise. It meant accompanying a work as it emerged. Our dialogue moves constantly between what Amina discovers through matter, how she deconstructs signs and symbols and what I bring through research and conceptual development. I would say the spatial development of the exhibition is where we meet. Venice gave that ongoing conversation another scale. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, installation view. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.caption: Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, installation view. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.text: Asǝṭṭa refers to ritual weaving, but the project approaches weaving as more than a material process — as a means through which knowledge, relationships and memory are constructed. How did this understanding of weaving develop between you?

AA: This question is similar to the first , so I will explain my process here. My entry point to weaving was through architecture and design, then two decades of fieldwork interacting with artisans across different regions. This process involves building trust, experimenting with materials, and collecting stories.

MB: For me, it became clearer through watching how knowledge circulates the loom. Everything happens before the first thread is stretched: preparing and washing the wool, spending time together, exchanging stories. Then comes the concentration of weaving itself, and the rituals that mark its beginning and completion. In several Moroccan cultures, woven work is understood through the cycle of a living being. That changes how one thinks about an object and the relationships it carries.

This understanding also shaped the exhibition. We wanted to give space to the time of making, to the pauses and transitions that allow a relationship to develop. The threshold became important here: entering a workshop, being welcomed, learning to look. The visitor enters another part of that process. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, detail. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.caption: Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, detail. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.text: The work emerges through relationships with spinners, embroiderers, basket-makers, jewellers, apprentices and master artisans. When many people hold and transmit knowledge, how do you think about authorship, and whose presence remains visible in the finished work?

AA: What is visible and what is experienced are two different things – there is an intangible presence that permeates the work. Everybody who contributed to this project is present, in the work, in the catalogue, in the signage. But the true presence is intangible: the gesture, the trust between artist and artisan, curator and exhibition designers, the atelier chief and head of production, the multisensory experience of raw wool, light, and metal. This human gesture and interaction with matter creates an energy of love and integrity.

MB: What can I add to that? Perhaps one story that stays with me. Yamna, a master weaver from the Khemisset region, produces a weave so tight that it cannot be embroidered. Amina responded to this particular quality by rethinking its place within the installation. To me, this says a great deal about how the work takes shape collectively: one person’s way of working the thread can redirect the composition. Yamna’s presence is there, in the density of her weave and in the form it helped bring into being. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, detail. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.caption: Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, detail. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.text: Language around craft and heritage can easily become nostalgic, particularly through terms such as “ancestral” and “traditional”. How do you resist fixing these practices in the past and recognise them as changing, inventive and contemporary forms of knowledge?

AA: I don’t see these terms as nostalgic. Without tradition, one cannot innovate. My artistic approach is to explore materiality and test hypotheses. This question rests on a common misconception: that working in textiles, for example, is somehow craft rather than painting or sculpture.

MB: I share Amina’s reluctance to treat these words as inherently nostalgic. What concerns me is the assumption that a practice becomes contemporary only once an artist takes an interest in it. The people who carry these skills are already experimenting, adjusting to materials, teaching and making decisions in the present. Working with Amina has made me question the hierarchies through which we recognise those decisions. Why should thought be readily attributed to one medium and reduced to dexterity in another? In Asǝṭṭa, inherited techniques shape how the work thinks and takes form.

The âatba , or threshold, sits at the conceptual centre of Asǝṭṭa—between inside and outside, private and public, sacred and profane. Why did the threshold become so important to the work, and does it offer a way of thinking about how knowledge moves between different worlds?

AA: Threshold is the architectural concept of transition – negative space or in-between space. This is what interests me. When you enter the artisan’s space, they welcome you into their practice, which is an intimate experience. That is what Asetta offers the viewer: an invitation into a private space where I tell stories. The curatorial intention is to graft a second skin onto the existing environment of the Arsenale in which multiple installations succeed one another. The skin is composed of a series of vertical bands that detach from the walls, creating spaces of passage where stories take place.

MB: The âatba is foundational to Asǝṭṭa . It also runs through Amina’s practice, particularly her relationship to space, which owes much to her first life as an architect. She pays attention to how we enter a place, how we move through it, what it reveals or holds back. In Asǝṭṭa, the threshold acquires depth; it becomes a space we can inhabit, and this shapes our encounter with the work.

For me, this resonates with Abdelkébir Khatibi’s resistance to fixed ideas of identity, his way of thinking different inheritances together. Knowledge moves through people, places and encounters, and changes along the way. The threshold gives us a way to consider those transformations while remaining attentive to the particular histories each person brings. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, installation view. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.caption: Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, installation view. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.text: Asǝṭṭa brings practices and relationships rooted in particular Moroccan places into one of contemporary art’s most international settings. How much needs to be translated for a Venice audience, and what do you deliberately allow to remain culturally specific or not immediately accessible?

AA: There is no intention to translate the work to the viewer – there is only the invitation to enter and create their own experience. A poetry of human interaction unfolds, evoking moments of curiosity. Interstices, for example, is a series of silver elements inserted between the bricks of a former passageway. These delicately crafted pieces are placed there to reactivate the closure, inviting a curious observer to examine it further.

Viewers might experience the entire installation or each work, with sunlight filtering through woven bands, or pause in their journey. One of the works, L’guelssa, is a place to rest, to contemplate, where the viewer becomes performer. The artist activates the vertical space of Interstices, while the viewer activates the horizontal space of L’guelssa.

MB: There is a distinction between offering context and explaining everything in advance. We can give visitors names, places and an account of how the work was made, while allowing their first encounter to remain sensory. The light, the weight of wool, the distance between two modules or the possibility of sitting down can already establish a relationship.

We wanted to retain words such as âatba and Asǝṭṭa because no English equivalent carries all their associations. Those associations can open gradually. Visitors arrive with their own memories of textiles, domestic spaces or protective objects; these may produce connections we could not anticipate.

The work is also specifically in conversation with Venice. The histories explored around the shriâa and the Venetian Rosetta suggest how an object can travel and take on new meanings. That possibility of transformation interests me more than making everything immediately familiar. Curator Meriem Berrada and Artist Amina Agueznay, Aseṭṭa . Created by artist Amina Agueznay. Courtesy of the Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication of the Kingdom of Morocco © Matteo Losurdo

blocks.caption: Curator Meriem Berrada and Artist Amina Agueznay, Aseṭṭa . Created by artist Amina Agueznay. Courtesy of the Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication of the Kingdom of Morocco © Matteo Losurdo

blocks.text: A national pavilion places an artwork within the framework of representing a country. Morocco contains multiple languages, regions, histories and cultural traditions. How do you work within that framework while resisting the expectation that a single project can stand for “Morocco”?

AA: This seems to be a misinterpretation of representation – whose expectation do you refer to? The intention is not to depict Morocco, but to offer an artistic vision that deserves the distinction of representing Morocco. Asetta is not about exalting a single aspect of Morocco, nor should it be. I’m the first artist to represent Morocco in Venice, but I won’t be the last.

MB: I approach that responsibility with precision in the proposal. We submitted a project grounded in Amina’s practice, in relationships developed over many years, in an encounter with this particular site and in the specific resonance with the “minor keys” conceptual framework. That is the basis on which I can speak as a curator.

Morocco’s plurality is already present in the work, through the different regions, materials, techniques, and individual trajectories that meet within it. We did not need to assign each of them a representative role. Their differences shape the forms themselves. I hope this pavilion makes room for a demanding artistic proposition to be encountered on its own terms, and opens possibilities for what follows. A first pavilion’s responsibility includes leaving that space open. Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, detail. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.caption: Amina Agueznay, Asǝṭṭa, 2026, detail. Courtesy of the Moroccan Ministry of Youth, Culture and Communication ©️ Ayoub El Bardii

blocks.text: In Minor Keys asks us to attend to quieter narratives and ways of knowing, while Asǝṭṭa takes monumental form. How do monumentality and the “minor” coexist in the installation, and can something monumental still direct attention to gestures, labour and knowledge that have historically remained less visible?

AA: Asǝṭṭa is indeed monumental in scale and scope. In fact, it was originally conceived as a monumental loom within the exhibition space – in which woven bands are stretched to create membrane and thresholds.

For me, the essence of “minor” lies in the musical reference. Works in major key resonate as affirmed, or resolved, whereas works in minor key are more introspective. This distinction speaks to me. With Asetta, we created a large-scale environment in which gesture and craft create intervals and rhythms—a way of experiencing the world.

MB: When I read Koyo Kouoh’s concept, I immediately thought of Amina. Her work develops a force through restraint, through attention to gestures and materials one might otherwise pass by. That affinity was central to our decision to propose the project.

For me, the question is where the monumentality takes you. In Asǝṭṭa , a view of the whole leads you towards a knot, a piece of beadwork, a change in the density of a weave. Moving closer changes the scale again. The intervals matter as much as the accumulation: they allow the eye and the body to pause.

The installation gives these gestures a spatial presence large enough to inhabit, while asking for an intimate kind of attention. I hear the resonance with “In Minor Keys” in that invitation to spend time with what is usually less visible, and to recognise the people and knowledge that sustain it.
